_comment: Labelled evaluation set. Copy to labels.json and replace with questions
you already know the answer to in YOUR corpus.
This is the only way to tell whether a change to the chunker, the
embedding model or the rerank instruction made retrieval better or merely
different. Eyeballing a result list cannot: it looks plausible either way.
expect_any: the case PASSES if any of these URIs appears in the results.
reject:     URIs that must NOT outrank the expected one. This is the
harder half. Surfacing the right note is easy; refusing the
plausible wrong one is where retrieval is actually won.
URIs are what search returns: 'fs:relative/path.md' for files,
'twenty:person/<id>' for CRM records.
A note that is a checklist or a list of links may be unfindable no
matter how you chunk it, because embedding models are trained on prose.
Give that note an 'about:' line in its frontmatter rather than tuning
retrieval around it. See the README.
Keep it small and real. Twelve questions you actually asked beat a
hundred invented ones, but note that a set this size cannot resolve an
MRR difference under about 0.05: one case is worth 1/12 of the metric.
expect_none: the corpus genuinely cannot answer this, and the case
passes when NOTHING clears the threshold. Without these,
every case rewards finding something, so a change that
made retrieval more eager would improve every number
while making the system worse in the way users notice.

cases.query: how do I roll back a failed deployment
what did we decide about the pricing model
which vendor did we rule out and why
what is the capital of Mongolia
what is the boiling point of mercury
how do I replace the timing belt on a Volvo 240
